steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Rich Romans lived in domus (single-family houses) with atrium, peristyle gardens and private baths

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Most Romans lived in insulae (multi-storey apartment blocks) — cramped, fire-prone and overcrowded

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: The typical Roman day began at dawn, with business conducted in the morning and leisure in the afternoon

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Roman meals: ientaculum (breakfast), prandium (light lunch), cena (main evening meal)

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Q: How did housing differ between rich and poor Romans? | Q: Why were the Roman baths so important socially? | Q: What did ordinary Romans eat?

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: The wealthy lived in domus — spacious single-family houses with gardens and private facilities. The poor lived in insulae — cramped, multi-storey blocks with shared facilities, no running water and hi | They were not just for washing — they were community centres for exercise, socialising, conducting business, relaxing and even studying. Going to the baths was a daily ritual for most Romans. | Breakfast (ientaculum) was bread and cheese; lunch (prandium) was light — leftovers or street food; dinner (cena) was the main meal — porridge, vegetables, bread and occasionally meat or fish for thos

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Always contrast rich and poor experiences — Roman life was deeply divided by wealth Use specific details: names of rooms (atrium, triclinium), food items, clothing types The baths are one of the best-evidenced aspects of daily Roman life — use them extensively Don't romanticise Roman life — insulae were dangerous and uncomfortable for most residents Link daily life to social structure — the way people lived reflected and reinforced their status
